chapters.title: Chapter 2: The New Toolkit of Economic Statecraft

lessons.title: Reshoring, Nearshoring and Friendshoring: Industrial Policy Goes Global

children.text: For thirty years, the default question a multinational asked when deciding where to manufacture was simple: where is it cheapest? From roughly 2018 onward, a second question forced its way into every boardroom alongside it: where is it safe? Governments stopped waiting for companies to answer that second question on their own. Washington, Brussels and New Delhi each built large, direct subsidy programmes to pull manufacturing toward locations they consider secure, and the vocabulary that describes this shift, reshoring, nearshoring, friendshoring, is not interchangeable jargon. Each word describes a different location decision, and each is backed by a different set of incentives you need to be able to name.

body.text: Industrial policy did not replace the market's cost logic. It added a second variable, political alignment, and then governments started paying companies directly to weight that second variable more heavily.

cells: Moving production to a foreign country mainly for lower cost, regardless of political alignment
A US company moving assembly to China in the 2000s purely on cost
Moving production back to the home country
A US company bringing chip fabrication back to Arizona or Ohio
Moving production to a geographically nearby country
A US company shifting assembly from China to Mexico
Moving production to a politically aligned country, regardless of geographic distance
A US company shifting sourcing from China to India or Vietnam

markDefs.definition: A term popularised by US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen in an April 2022 speech, describing the deliberate concentration of supply chains among politically aligned or trusted trading partners, rather than purely on cost or geographic proximity.

children.text: Friendshoring is the newest and broadest of these terms, popularised by US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen in an April 2022 speech that explicitly framed

as a response to the vulnerabilities exposed by COVID-19 and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It is the term that best describes why India, geographically nowhere near the United States, has still become one of the largest beneficiaries of this shift.
The US CHIPS and Science Act

Signed into law in August 2022, the CHIPS and Science Act committed roughly $52.7 billion to semiconductor manufacturing incentives, research and workforce development, alongside a 25% investment tax credit for chip fabrication equipment. The intent was explicit reshoring: rebuild a domestic manufacturing base for a technology the US had, over three decades, allowed to concentrate heavily in Taiwan and South Korea. Within two years, TSMC had committed to invest tens of billions of dollars in new Arizona fabs, Samsung committed a similarly large sum to a new campus in Taylor, Texas, and Intel announced a major new manufacturing hub in Ohio it publicly branded its "Silicon Heartland."

children.text: Europe chose deliberately different language from Washington's more confrontational posture. In a March 2023 speech ahead of a visit to Beijing, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen framed the EU's approach as "de-risking, not decoupling," reducing dependency on any single supplier for strategically critical goods without severing trade with China altogether. The European Chips Act, adopted the same year, aims to mobilise roughly €43 billion in public and private investment by 2030, targeting a doubling of the EU's share of global chip production from around 10% to 20%. A parallel Critical Raw Materials Act sets similar diversification targets for minerals used in batteries, magnets and renewable energy equipment, a theme Chapter 5 of this course returns to in depth.

body.text: "De-risking, not decoupling" is now the standard phrase used across G7 communiques and Indian trade policy discussions alike. It signals a deliberate choice: reduce concentration risk in critical sectors while keeping the broader trading relationship with China intact, closer to the rerouting pattern this course documented in Chapter 1 than to a full economic break.

children.text: India's PLI Schemes: Friendshoring's Largest Beneficiary

India built its own version of this playbook starting in 2020: Production Linked Incentive schemes that pay manufacturers a percentage of incremental sales in exchange for meeting production and investment targets on Indian soil. The programme expanded to 14 sectors with a combined outlay of roughly ₹1.97 lakh crore, a little over $26 billion. The single largest and most visible success has been large-scale electronics manufacturing: Apple's assembly partners, Foxconn, Pegatron and, since Tata Group's 2023 acquisition of Wistron's Karnataka plant, Tata Electronics itself, have scaled iPhone assembly in India sharply, with the government reporting India's iPhone exports crossing roughly $10 billion in the 2023-24 financial year. A separate India Semiconductor Mission, announced in December 2021 with an outlay of roughly ₹76,000 crore, aims to build fabrication and packaging capacity domestically, a subject Chapter 4 covers in far more detail.

body.title: Name the mechanism
body.textWithBlank: Shifting production to a politically aligned country regardless of geographic distance, the term US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen popularised in April 2022, is called ___.
body.explanation: Friendshoring is distinct from nearshoring, which is specifically about geographic proximity. India benefiting from US and European supply chain diversification despite the distance involved is a textbook friendshoring example, not nearshoring.

children.text: The evidence so far is mixed, and a macro investor should treat any single success story with some caution. India's electronics PLI has clearly worked by its own metrics, exports and domestic production both scaled quickly. Other PLI sectors have seen slower, more uneven uptake, and globally, subsidy-driven reshoring raises two structural concerns worth tracking as this plays out over the next decade.

When the US, EU, India, Japan and South Korea are all subsidising the same industries simultaneously, the result can be duplicated capacity and demand for the same skilled engineers and equipment across multiple countries at once, raising costs for everyone rather than efficiently reshoring supply.

Large, targeted production subsidies sit uneasily with WTO rules on prohibited and actionable subsidies, and several of these programmes, including aspects of India's own PLI structure, have already drawn formal or informal scrutiny from trading partners.

body.title: Classify the shift
body.question: A US electronics brand moves assembly from a factory in China to a new facility in Vietnam, purely because Vietnam offers lower labour costs than China now does, with no reference to political alignment. What is this best described as?
options: A continuation of ordinary offshoring, now just relocated within Asia
body.explanation: Without a political alignment rationale, moving from one low-cost Asian manufacturing base to another is still offshoring in its classic sense, cost-driven relocation. Friendshoring specifically requires the alignment rationale, reshoring requires returning to the home country, and Vietnam is not geographically near the US, so nearshoring does not fit either.

cards.definition: Moving production back to the company's home country.
Moving production to a geographically nearby country, such as US firms shifting to Mexico.
Moving production to a politically aligned or trusted country regardless of geographic distance, the term Janet Yellen popularised in April 2022.

India's scheme paying manufacturers a percentage of incremental sales for meeting production and investment targets domestically, spanning 14 sectors with a combined outlay of roughly ₹1.97 lakh crore.
The EU's preferred framing, distinct from decoupling, for reducing dependency on a single supplier in strategic sectors while keeping the broader trading relationship intact.

points: Reshoring, nearshoring and friendshoring describe three distinct location decisions, home country, nearby country and politically aligned country respectively, not synonyms for the same trend.
The US CHIPS Act committed roughly $52.7 billion to reshore semiconductor manufacturing, drawing tens of billions of dollars in new fab investment from TSMC, Samsung and Intel.
The EU frames its approach as de-risking, not decoupling, backed by a Chips Act targeting €43 billion in mobilised investment and a doubling of its global chip production share by 2030.
India's PLI schemes, roughly ₹1.97 lakh crore across 14 sectors, made India one of friendshoring's largest beneficiaries, most visibly in Apple's iPhone assembly shift.
Industrial policy's track record is mixed so far, with real risks of duplicated global capacity from simultaneous subsidy races and growing friction with WTO subsidy rules.

Not every factory relocation is friendshoring or reshoring. A purely cost-driven move between two low-cost countries is still ordinary offshoring, and the distinction matters for reading what a company's supply chain announcement actually signals.
